summary: Describes generic requirements for provider provisioned virtual private networks, split into service, provider and engineering requirements. They apply to all PPVPN technologies. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Companies rent private networks from providers. This lists what any such service must do, no matter how it is built.

questions: how do l2vpn and l3vpn differ
what does pe-based and ce-based mean
subtitle: The complete set of requirements that any provider-provisioned VPN service must meet.

tldr.problem: Service providers deploy Virtual Private Networks with different technologies, but customers need consistent capabilities regardless of how VPNs are built.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC catalogs generic requirements that all Provider Provisioned VPNs must satisfy, covering service features, provider scalability needs, and engineering implementation details.
tldr.outcome: The requirements enable service providers to deploy multiple VPN technologies (Layer 2 and Layer 3, CE-based and PE-based) while meeting customer expectations for availability, security, and performance.

facts.label: VPN types covered
facts.value: Layer 2 and Layer 3, PE-based and CE-based

today: These generic requirements have guided development of PPVPN solutions including BGP/MPLS IP VPNs (RFC 2547), VPLS, and various Layer 2 VPN approaches. Service providers now offer all three deployment scenarios: single-provider single-AS VPNs (most common), single-provider multi-AS VPNs (for large providers), and multi-provider VPNs (increasingly deployed as enterprises expand globally). Understanding these requirements remains essential for evaluating new VPN technologies and solutions.

sections.title: Why Generic PPVPN Requirements Matter
sections.content:
Organizations increasingly depend on networks to connect their sites. Provider Provisioned Virtual Private Networks (PPVPNs) deliver this connectivity over shared infrastructure: an ISP runs the network and customers rent virtual connections between their locations. Service providers historically offered Frame Relay or ATM; now they offer multiple technologies including Ethernet, IP tunnels, and MPLS.

The problem: each technology works differently internally, and customers cannot switch providers without replacing their equipment if each provider implements VPNs differently. This RFC defines a common set of requirements that all PPVPN services must meet, regardless of the underlying technology. This allows customers to compare services and switch providers, and allows service providers to choose between technologies without losing interoperability.
sections.eli5: When companies rent private networks from ISPs, they want the same service no matter what technology is used inside. This document lists what every rented private network must do.

sections.title: Kinds of PPVPNs and Service Requirements
sections.content:
PPVPNs split into two broad categories: Layer 2 VPNs (L2VPN) connect sites as if they were on the same local network, forwarding Ethernet frames between them. Layer 3 VPNs (L3VPN) route IP packets between sites. Each category further divides into PE-based (Provider Equipment handles VPN logic) and CE-based (Customer Equipment handles VPN logic).

From a customer perspective, PPVPNs must deliver high availability: connectivity persists even when network components fail, achieved through physical redundancy or backup tunnels. They must be stable: routing neither flaps nor loops, and the service remains intact during upgrades. They must support unicast traffic (point-to-point) and ideally multicast and broadcast (point-to-multipoint). They must isolate customer data: packets never cross VPN boundaries unless customers explicitly agree to share (as in an extranet). They must enforce security: user data is encrypted, customer sites are authenticated, and denial-of-service attacks are mitigated.
sections.eli5: Rented networks can work different ways: some forward frames like local networks, others route packets like the Internet. Both types need to keep working when things break, handle different kinds of traffic, and keep customers' data separate.

sections.title: Service Features and Scalability Demands
sections.content:
PPVPNs must support predictable topology and addressing. A customer might want a full mesh (every site connected to every other), a hub-and-spoke (all traffic through one site), or a partial mesh. The service must support both IPv4 and IPv6, and customers must be able to address their sites without coordination with other customers (requiring isolation). Quality of Service matters: customers may need bandwidth guarantees or traffic prioritization. Service Level Agreements specify uptime percentages and performance metrics; the provider must monitor and report on them.

From the provider's perspective, scalability dominates. A large service provider must support O(10^4) VPNs concurrently. Each VPN might have few or over 50,000 sites. Routes per VPN range from a handful to O(10^5). Redundancy increases these demands further. A VPN solution must handle not only bulk scaling on the high end but also cost-effective operation on the low end: a three-site VPN with three users should be as viable as a 1000-site enterprise network. When VPNs span multiple service providers, management complexity grows exponentially; solutions must articulate their limits in these scenarios.
sections.eli5: Customers need predictable networks: specific topologies, addressing that does not collide, traffic that goes where promised, and documented service quality. Providers need to support thousands of VPNs simultaneously, from tiny to enormous, all profitable to operate.

sections.title: Engineering and Control Planes
sections.content:
Forwarding plane requirements govern how packets move. Customer packets MUST be kept in their VPN; the provider MUST NOT mix traffic across VPN boundaries. The forwarding plane must support the topologies customers choose without loops or unnecessary delays. Control plane requirements govern how routing information flows. In PE-based VPNs, the PE learns routes from connected customer equipment and distributes them to other PEs in that VPN, but NOT to PEs in other VPNs. In CE-based VPNs, CEs exchange routing information through a tunnel established by the provider network.

A key principle: control plane containment means that the core network (provider backbone) need not maintain per-VPN information about customer routes. Instead, PEs at the network edge aggregate customer information, keeping the core simple and scalable. Solutions SHOULD be as compatible as possible with standard Internet mechanisms (discovery, signaling, routing, management) without overloading them.
sections.eli5: Packets must stay in their own VPN and never leak. The provider's backbone routers should not have to remember details about each customer's network; the edge routers handle that.

sections.title: Management, Security, and Multi-Provider Scenarios
sections.content:
PPVPNs must be manageable: customers SHOULD be able to configure and monitor their own VPNs through a management interface provided by the service provider. Configuration changes (adding or removing sites) must be rapid, particularly for on-demand services like temporary videoconferencing VPNs.

Security mechanisms protect customer data using encryption, authentication, and access controls. Denial-of-service attacks (TCP SYN floods, ping attacks, attacks on router CPUs) MUST be mitigated. Some mechanisms like CE-to-CE IPsec work across all deployment scenarios; others apply only to certain scopes. Multi-provider VPNs, where the PPVPN spans multiple service providers, demand trust negotiations and coordinated Service Level Agreements; such deployments are the most complex and require explicit provider-to-provider agreements.

The requirements intentionally remain technology-agnostic. Both MPLS-based L3VPNs and Ethernet-based L2VPNs, both PE-based and CE-based solutions, can meet these requirements. This flexibility allows service providers to invest in multiple technologies, drivers competition, and lets customers switch providers without wholesale network redesign.
sections.eli5: Customers need to manage their own networks. Data must be encrypted and attacks stopped. When VPNs cross multiple providers, everyone has to agree on what the service will be.
